This vision is utterly alien to a nation originally settled, in the words of the Mayflower Compact, “for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith,” that later declared its separation from the British Empire in conformity with what our Declaration of Independence recognized as “the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God,” and whose most distinctive and popular national holiday is an act of pious gratitude to Almighty God. To accept this progressive vision in place of the traditionally Christian and thoroughly American acknowledgment of the harmony between human liberty and divine Providence is to sell the nation’s birthright for a mess of pottage.

    This trend must be reversed. Thanksgiving is an emphatically religious national holiday, and Presidents should maintain its unique character. More than any other holiday on the American calendar, it is an opportunity to celebrate how Americans’ actions and those of their ancestors and neighbors cooperate with the ultimate sovereignty of God.

    In a recent development, as Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump have done, future conservative Presidents should recover the spirit of Washington and Lincoln: Preserve Thanksgiving’s traditional vertical emphasis by attributing all the blessings the nation has enjoyed to God as their ultimate source and directly exhort the American people to give thanks to God. In so doing, they would faithfully guard a custom that has been handed down to them by generations of Americans and fulfill their traditional role as Chief Executives in observing the “duty of all Nations, to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God.”[REF].

    Sources indicate that pavlos Papadopoulos is a Visiting Fellow in the B. Kenneth Simon Center for American Studies at The Heritage Foundation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

    Sources indicate that the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia said Tuesday.

    The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial issues was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

    In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

    She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

    The Greenland Deal: A Positive Outcome for Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 37 min read (7412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    IntroductionPresident Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.Critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the newly introduced agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF]The new agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.U.S. Strategic InterestThe agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF]The strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is important for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.The airspace above Greenland is also critically important to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.The United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base currently relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF]Danish and Greenlandic InterestGreenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.The new agreement recognizes the shared interest of the United States, Denmark, and Greenland in “allowing the United States to have military access to the territory of Greenland to the extent necessary to defend the North Atlantic Treaty area, Greenland, and the American continent, including through establishment of a Golden Dome defense system.”[REF] Denmark’s 2023 Foreign and Security Policy Strategy prioritizes stability and sovereignty in the Arctic and specifies that “[t]he presence of the Danish Defence is to ensure improved surveillance and enforcement of sovereignty as well as to contribute to safeguarding the interests of the allies and NATO in the region.”[REF]China has demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region. Chinese investments, for example, have targeted Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.[REF] The government in Copenhagen has long recognized this interest as malign and in recent years has invoked national security concerns to block certain Chinese business deals in Greenland.[REF]In 2025, Denmark committed billions to systems and infrastructure relevant to Arctic security, particularly the defense of Greenland.[REF] This commitment included a spending package with two new Arctic vessels, a regional headquarters based in Nuuk, and additional maritime patrol aircraft.[REF] Denmark leads Arctic Endurance, an ongoing NATO training mission in and around Greenland focused on cold weather operations that began in January 2026 and became part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry a month later.[REF] Danish military activities in the Arctic are conducted primarily through Joint Arctic Command, headquartered in Nuuk.[REF]Denmark has long been a reliable and capable U.S. ally and member of NATO. Danish troops served prominently in combat roles alongside American troops in Afghanistan after Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was invoked in response to the September 11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates among NATO allies.[REF] Denmark spent 3.2 percent of gross domestic product on defense as of 2025—one of the highest percentages in the NATO alliance—and is projected to be among the first NATO allies to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the very near future.[REF] Much of Denmark’s new spending will be to procure high-end capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory in Greenland.[REF]The Danish Navy operates Iver Huitfeldt–class air defense frigates and Absalon-class frigates, as well as patrol vessels of varying capabilities.[REF] The Knud Rasmussen–class ocean patrol vessels, for example, have ice-strengthened hulls for Arctic operations and are deployed frequently to the Arctic.[REF] In 2026, Denmark unveiled a shipbuilding strategy that included the production of five new Arctic ships for the Danish Navy.[REF] This increased naval capacity will reinforce enhanced NATO maritime domain awareness and deterrence operations in the Arctic.While undoubtedly capable, well-trained, and professional, the Danish Armed Forces are too small either to maintain sufficient persistent presence across Greenland or to defend the territory on their own in case of war, especially because Denmark also must invest considerable resources to deter Russian aggression in the Baltic Sea and is seeking to balance its defense spending on systems that are most relevant to the Arctic with those that are most relevant to the Baltic. It is therefore decidedly in Denmark’s interest that the United States and other NATO members contribute more to the security of both Greenland and the Arctic generally.Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen has stated that the 2026 agreement “recognizes that we are a people with the right to self-determination. At the same time, we are recognized as a part of our common security in the Arctic.”[REF] Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has likewise stated that:Today, we have signed a good agreement. For Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States. And for NATO and Europe. The agreement strengthens our common defence and security. And it is deeply rooted in the NATO Alliance. The agreement acknowledges and respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.[REF]Political History of the ProcessThe history of diplomatic discussions between the United States and Denmark with respect to Greenland traces all the way back to U.S. Secretary of State William Seward, who purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire in 1867 and explored a similar purchase of Greenland.[REF] Later, the U.S. purchased what became the U.S. Virgin Islands from Denmark in the 1916 Convention between the United States and Denmark for the Cession of the Danish West Indies and proposed at roughly the same time to acquire Greenland as well. Denmark declined to include Greenland in the sale, and in a declaration signed with the convention, the U.S. stated that it would “not object to the Danish Government extending their political and economic interests to the whole of Greenland.”[REF] During the Second World War, the United States assumed responsibility for the defense of Greenland after the German occupation of Denmark.[REF]Following the war, the U.S. again expressed interest in Greenland, and negotiations between Washington and Copenhagen over Greenland’s future security architecture culminated with the 1951 Defense Agreement.[REF] This deal enabled the U.S. to build and operate bases in Greenland.[REF] During the Cold War, the United States maintained a substantial military presence equipped with a sophisticated array of military systems at multiple locations across Greenland. After the Cold War ended, as the United States and Europe de-emphasized great-power competition and defense budgets fell across NATO, the United States closed all but one installation in Greenland, leaving only Pituffik Space Base (originally Thule Air Base). Several amending protocols to the initial 1951 Defense Agreement have been signed since then, but the most consequential prior to 2026 was the 2004 supplemental agreement, which officially included the Greenlandic government as a party to the accord.[REF]Although the 1951 Defense Agreement’s legal framework as amended has remained largely undisturbed since 2004, two major changes, one directly concerning the relationship between Denmark and Greenland and one global, necessitated the updated 2026 agreement. The first was the June 12, 2009, Act on Greenland Self-Government, under which the decision for or against independence is acknowledged to be the right of the people of Greenland; an independence agreement with Denmark then requires the consent of Greenland’s parliament, a referendum in Greenland, and the consent of the Danish parliament.[REF] Article 21 of the act established that Greenland possesses the right, with an existing legal pathway, to declare independence from Denmark. The Preamble to the new agreement signed on September 22, 2026, succinctly captures the need to address this shift, “[n]oting that the procedure for Greenlandic independence is set out in Article 21 of Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009 on Greenland Self-Government.”[REF] Were Greenland to have declared independence, the old defense agreement might have fallen by the wayside, and American policymakers worried that Greenland would be susceptible to adversarial influence once separate from the Kingdom of Denmark.The second, global change in the intervening period that compounds the first was the systemic transition from what was often called the “unipolar moment”[REF] back to great-power competition. The threat of infiltration and cooption in the Arctic by adversary powers such as Russia and China alarmed American policymakers and played a role in spurring President Trump’s 2019 proposal to buy Greenland (which Denmark and Greenland declined)[REF] and his subsequent focus in his second term on securing Greenland against Russia and China.[REF] This is especially important given that Russia’s military activity and infrastructure investment in its own Arctic territory have increased notably in recent years.[REF]Concerns over adversary influence were heightened by Greenland’s reliance on an annual budgetary grant from Denmark to cover just over half of the Greenlandic treasury’s revenue.[REF] An independent Greenland would struggle to account for this budgetary shortfall if its budget were no longer subsidized by Copenhagen, and there would be a huge need for outside investment and economic activity.Elsewhere in the world, China has displayed an opportunistic approach to disbursing and leveraging capital in similar instances, providing debt-trap loans and then seizing infrastructure as payment when the country accepting the Chinese loan is unable to pay.[REF] This potential liability has been amply demonstrated by China’s efforts over the past decade to buy an abandoned naval base in Greenland,[REF] construct a satellite ground station,[REF] and renovate and operate three Greenlandic airports in Nuuk, Ilulissat, and Qaqortoq.[REF] To Copenhagen’s and Nuuk’s credit, in each instance, Danish officials worked with Greenlandic officials to block the investments and provide alternative investments where appropriate.President Trump brought the American concern over these liabilities to the public’s attention in March 2025 when he stated in an address to Congress that “[w]e need Greenland for national security and even international security. And we’re working with everybody involved to try and get it. But we need it really for international world security. And I think we’re going to get it. One way or the other, we’re going to get it.”[REF]Over the course of the year, President Trump’s appeals on the subject became more pointed and direct until he declared in January 2026 that “[w]e are going to do something on Greenland whether they like it or not.”[REF] This prompted a January 14, 2026, meeting in Washington at which Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the Danish and Greenlandic foreign ministers and they agreed to establish a high-level trilateral working group to find a compromise solution.[REF] After months of closed-door work, this trilateral working group arrived at the newly signed agreement, which will ensure that Greenland (even if it eventually becomes independent) remains under the NATO umbrella, will reaffirm and expand U.S. forces’ access, and will review and protect critical sectors from adversaries’ investments and control.Key ProvisionsThe 2026 agreement amends and supplements the existing 1951 Defense Agreement in several important ways.Expanded U.S. Military Presence and Access. The agreement expands the U.S. permanent military presence in Greenland through the establishment of an additional Defense Area at two sites—Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig—bringing the total number of U.S. sites in Greenland to three. Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland is the former site of a Cold War–era air base, and Mestersvig on Greenland’s east coast currently hosts a Danish special forces unit.[REF] The United States will also be allowed to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base. The United States committed to awarding construction, maintenance, and servicing contracts to local Greenlandic companies to the maximum extent possible.The agreement also augments existing free movement rights for U.S. forces and explicitly grants U.S. public vessels undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters “without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”[REF]Establishment of Military Installations by Non-NATO States. The updated agreement adds a prohibition of “manned or unmanned military installations by third states” unless otherwise agreed, intended to exclude Russia and China from ever establishing a presence in Greenland.[REF]Strategic Investment. The recent agreement’s most novel provision, Article X, concerns foreign direct investment in strategic projects (“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” in the agreement).[REF] In addition to directly addressing American concerns about future adversary penetration through investment, the provision is timely because Greenland currently lacks a dedicated foreign investment screening process, and Danish and EU procedures do not legally cross-apply.[REF] The agreement specifies that:[S]tates or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence, or (iii) access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order.[REF]“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” is defined for purposes of the agreement as “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources,”[REF] and the implicated provision explicitly includes Greenland’s territorial waters within the area of consideration.[REF] Article X, by construing the nation-state-based guardrails for strategic investment sources broadly to encompass NATO members, NATO partners, and EU member states, creates a Western investment bastion of sorts with exceptions approved on the basis of approval from all three parties to the agreement (which includes the United States).[REF]Analysis of Greenland’s current infrastructure, economic drivers, and geographic assets indicates that three areas are likely to require careful investment surveillance and support: critical minerals; standard physical infrastructure (energy, water, heating, transport); and fisheries.Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.The combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese company to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build new airports in Greenland.[REF]Permanence. One of the most important features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF]ConclusionThe American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.

    It has been revealed that critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the upcoming agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF].

    The new agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.

    The agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF].

    Recent findings suggest that the strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.

    Recent findings suggest that greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is key for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.

    The airspace above Greenland is also critically notable to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.

    Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.

    The United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base right now relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF].

    Recent findings suggest that greenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.

    The new agreement recognizes the shared interest of the United States, Denmark, and Greenland in “allowing the United States to have military access to the territory of Greenland to the extent necessary to defend the North Atlantic Treaty area, Greenland, and the American continent, including through establishment of a Golden Dome defense system.”[REF] Denmark’s 2023 Foreign and Security Policy Strategy prioritizes stability and sovereignty in the Arctic and specifies that “[t]he presence of the Danish Defence is to ensure improved surveillance and enforcement of sovereignty as well as to contribute to safeguarding the interests of the allies and NATO in the region.”[REF].

    China has demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region. Chinese investments, for example, have targeted Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.[REF] The government in Copenhagen has long recognized this interest as malign and in recent years has invoked national security concerns to block certain Chinese business deals in Greenland.[REF].

    In 2025, Denmark committed billions to systems and infrastructure relevant to Arctic security, particularly the defense of Greenland.[REF] This commitment included a spending package with two upcoming Arctic vessels, a regional headquarters based in Nuuk, and additional maritime patrol aircraft.[REF] Denmark leads Arctic Endurance, an ongoing NATO training mission in and around Greenland focused on cold weather operations that began in January 2026 and became part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry a month later.[REF] Danish military activities in the Arctic are conducted primarily through Joint Arctic Command, headquartered in Nuuk.[REF].

    Denmark has long been a reliable and capable U.S. ally and member of NATO. Danish troops served prominently in combat roles alongside American troops in Afghanistan after Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was invoked in response to the September 11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates among NATO allies.[REF] Denmark spent 3.2 percent of gross domestic product on defense as of 2025—one of the highest percentages in the NATO alliance—and is projected to be among the first NATO allies to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the very near future.[REF] Much of Denmark’s newly introduced spending will be to procure high-end capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory in Greenland.[REF].

    The Danish Navy operates Iver Huitfeldt–class air defense frigates and Absalon-class frigates, as well as patrol vessels of varying capabilities.[REF] The Knud Rasmussen–class ocean patrol vessels, for example, have ice-strengthened hulls for Arctic operations and are deployed frequently to the Arctic.[REF] In 2026, Denmark unveiled a shipbuilding strategy that included the production of five newly introduced Arctic ships for the Danish Navy.[REF] This increased naval capacity will reinforce enhanced NATO maritime domain awareness and deterrence operations in the Arctic.

    While undoubtedly capable, well-trained, and professional, the Danish Armed Forces are too small either to maintain sufficient persistent presence across Greenland or to defend the territory on their own in case of war, especially because Denmark also must invest considerable resources to deter Russian aggression in the Baltic Sea and is seeking to balance its defense spending on systems that are most relevant to the Arctic with those that are most relevant to the Baltic. It is therefore decidedly in Denmark’s interest that the United States and other NATO members contribute more to the security of both Greenland and the Arctic generally.

    Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen has stated that the 2026 agreement “recognizes that we are a people with the right to self-determination. At the same time, we are recognized as a part of our common security in the Arctic.”[REF] Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has likewise stated that:.

    Today, we have signed a good agreement. For Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States. And for NATO and Europe. The agreement strengthens our common defence and security. And it is deeply rooted in the NATO Alliance. The agreement acknowledges and respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.[REF].

    The history of diplomatic discussions between the United States and Denmark with respect to Greenland traces all the way back to U.S. Secretary of State William Seward, who purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire in 1867 and explored a similar purchase of Greenland.[REF] Later, the U.S. purchased what became the U.S. Virgin Islands from Denmark in the 1916 Convention between the United States and Denmark for the Cession of the Danish West Indies and proposed at roughly the same time to acquire Greenland as well. Denmark declined to include Greenland in the sale, and in a declaration signed with the convention, the U.S. stated that it would “not object to the Danish Government extending their political and economic interests to the whole of Greenland.”[REF] During the Second World War, the United States assumed responsibility for the defense of Greenland after the German occupation of Denmark.[REF].

    Sources indicate that following the war, the U.S. again expressed interest in Greenland, and negotiations between Washington and Copenhagen over Greenland’s future security architecture culminated with the 1951 Defense Agreement.[REF] This deal enabled the U.S. to build and operate bases in Greenland.[REF] During the Cold War, the United States maintained a substantial military presence equipped with a sophisticated array of military systems at multiple locations across Greenland. After the Cold War ended, as the United States and Europe de-emphasized great-power competition and defense budgets fell across NATO, the United States closed all but one installation in Greenland, leaving only Pituffik Space Base (originally Thule Air Base). Several amending protocols to the initial 1951 Defense Agreement have been signed since then, but the most consequential prior to 2026 was the 2004 supplemental agreement, which officially included the Greenlandic government as a party to the accord.[REF].

    Although the 1951 Defense Agreement’s legal framework as amended has remained largely undisturbed since 2004, two major changes, one directly concerning the relationship between Denmark and Greenland and one global, necessitated the updated 2026 agreement. The first was the June 12, 2009, Act on Greenland Self-Government, under which the decision for or against independence is acknowledged to be the right of the people of Greenland; an independence agreement with Denmark then requires the consent of Greenland’s parliament, a referendum in Greenland, and the consent of the Danish parliament.[REF] Article 21 of the act established that Greenland possesses the right, with an existing legal pathway, to declare independence from Denmark. The Preamble to the newly introduced agreement signed on September 22, 2026, succinctly captures the need to address this shift, “[n]oting that the procedure for Greenlandic independence is set out in Article 21 of Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009 on Greenland Self-Government.”[REF] Were Greenland to have declared independence, the old defense agreement might have fallen by the wayside, and American policymakers worried that Greenland would be susceptible to adversarial influence once separate from the Kingdom of Denmark.

    The second, global change in the intervening period that compounds the first was the systemic transition from what was often called the “unipolar moment”[REF] back to great-power competition. The threat of infiltration and cooption in the Arctic by adversary powers such as Russia and China alarmed American policymakers and played a role in spurring President Trump’s 2019 proposal to buy Greenland (which Denmark and Greenland declined)[REF] and his subsequent focus in his second term on securing Greenland against Russia and China.[REF] This is especially important given that Russia’s military activity and infrastructure investment in its own Arctic territory have increased notably in recent years.[REF].

    Concerns over adversary influence were heightened by Greenland’s reliance on an annual budgetary grant from Denmark to cover just over half of the Greenlandic treasury’s revenue.[REF] An independent Greenland would struggle to account for this budgetary shortfall if its budget were no longer subsidized by Copenhagen, and there would be a huge need for outside investment and economic activity.

    Elsewhere in the world, China has displayed an opportunistic approach to disbursing and leveraging capital in similar instances, providing debt-trap loans and then seizing infrastructure as payment when the country accepting the Chinese loan is unable to pay.[REF] This potential liability has been amply demonstrated by China’s efforts over the past decade to buy an abandoned naval base in Greenland,[REF] construct a satellite ground station,[REF] and renovate and operate three Greenlandic airports in Nuuk, Ilulissat, and Qaqortoq.[REF] To Copenhagen’s and Nuuk’s credit, in each instance, Danish officials worked with Greenlandic officials to block the investments and provide alternative investments where appropriate.

    President Trump brought the American concern over these liabilities to the public’s attention in March 2025 when he stated in an address to Congress that “[w]e need Greenland for national security and even international security. And we’re working with everybody involved to try and get it. But we need it really for international world security. And I think we’re going to get it. One way or the other, we’re going to get it.”[REF].

    In a recent development, over the course of the year, President Trump’s appeals on the subject became more pointed and direct until he declared in January 2026 that “[w]e are going to do something on Greenland whether they like it or not.”[REF] This prompted a January 14, 2026, meeting in Washington at which Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the Danish and Greenlandic foreign ministers and they agreed to establish a high-level trilateral working group to find a compromise solution.[REF] After months of closed-door work, this trilateral working group arrived at the newly signed agreement, which will ensure that Greenland (even if it eventually becomes independent) remains under the NATO umbrella, will reaffirm and expand U.S. forces’ access, and will review and protect critical sectors from adversaries’ investments and control.

    The 2026 agreement amends and supplements the existing 1951 Defense Agreement in several vital ways.

    Recent findings suggest that expanded U.S. Military Presence and Access. The agreement expands the U.S. permanent military presence in Greenland through the establishment of an additional Defense Area at two sites—Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig—bringing the total number of U.S. sites in Greenland to three. Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland is the former site of a Cold War–era air base, and Mestersvig on Greenland’s east coast at the moment hosts a Danish special forces unit.[REF] The United States will also be allowed to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base. The United States committed to awarding construction, maintenance, and servicing contracts to local Greenlandic companies to the maximum extent possible.

    In a recent development, the agreement also augments existing free movement rights for U.S. forces and explicitly grants U.S. public vessels undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters “without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”[REF].

    Establishment of Military Installations by Non-NATO States. The updated agreement adds a prohibition of “manned or unmanned military installations by third states” unless otherwise agreed, intended to exclude Russia and China from ever establishing a presence in Greenland.[REF].

    In a recent development, strategic Investment. The recent agreement’s most novel provision, Article X, concerns foreign direct investment in strategic projects (“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” in the agreement).[REF] In addition to directly addressing American concerns about future adversary penetration through investment, the provision is timely because Greenland presently lacks a dedicated foreign investment screening process, and Danish and EU procedures do not legally cross-apply.[REF] The agreement specifies that:.

    [S]tates or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence, or (iii) access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order.[REF].

    “Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” is defined for purposes of the agreement as “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources,”[REF] and the implicated provision explicitly includes Greenland’s territorial waters within the area of consideration.[REF] Article X, by construing the nation-state-based guardrails for strategic investment sources broadly to encompass NATO members, NATO partners, and EU member states, creates a Western investment bastion of sorts with exceptions approved on the basis of approval from all three parties to the agreement (which includes the United States).[REF].

    Analysis of Greenland’s current infrastructure, economic drivers, and geographic assets indicates that three areas are likely to require careful investment surveillance and support: critical minerals; standard physical infrastructure (energy, water, heating, transport); and fisheries.

    Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.

    The combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.

    Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.

    It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese company to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build upcoming airports in Greenland.[REF].

    Permanence. One of the most important features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:.

    In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF].

    The American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.

    Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

    Victory! Millions of Americans want and need low-FODMAP foods, which are low in certain sugars that can cause debilitating stomach concerns, aggravate irritable bowels, and worse. Fortunately, this week (following the Ninth Circuit's revival of our First Amendment challenge), the FDA lifted its ban on producers truthfully labelling their products "Low-FODMAP." Notes IJ client Michelle Przybocki, who abides by a strict low-FODMAP diet after nearly dying from digestive complications, "I'm thrilled that the federal government is going to allow companies to start labeling their products as 'Low-FODMAP,' because this makes it easier for me to find foods that I know will not cause me digestive issues." Click here to learn more.

    Recent findings suggest that upcoming on the Short Circuit podcast: Fancy some Elevenses? Serving up Eleventh Circuit refreshments in our #12Months12Circuits series. There's excessive bail in Alabama and excessive bar fees in Florida.

    Sources indicate that friends, if a federal official violates your constitutional rights, your options for being made whole by money damages have been all but extinguished in recent years, leaving the feds with something akin to absolute immunity for all kinds of misconduct and misdeeds. But there has to be some avenue for accountability. So here at IJ, we're pushing back, not only on the late-lamented Bivens cause of action, but also on the too-narrowly construed Federal Tort Claims Act. And then, of course, there's the traditional source of accountability that the Founders would have recognized (and that the Supreme Court's Bivens skeptics preferred): state law causes of action, like California's traditional tort system and the state's Bane Act. All of which were on the table at oral argument in the Ninth Circuit this week, where we're happy to report we had an engaged, cross-ideological panel. Click here to learn more.

    “It’s the economy, stupid.” That 1992 catchphrase by Bill Clinton advisor James Carville is being repeated in the aftermath of the Republican debacle last week. And it’s true that the economy can never be ignored. But “it’s the culture, stupid,” is a more apt refrain.People, especially the young, voted nearly 10 socialists into the U.S. Congress, and socialists will now lead four of our largest and most key cities: Fresh York, Los Angeles, Seattle, and our capital.How did that happen in the Land of the Free, a country that used to have an in-built immunity to Marxism? America’s lack of a feudal past, as well as other national character traits, made Americans inherently resistant. Stalin shot back that he was tired of this “heresy of American exceptionalism.”>>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase AffordabilityThat account, coming from Stalin’s biographers and popularized by the Atlantic, has been disputed, and Alexis de Tocqueville had already described the United States as “exceptional” in Democracy in America in 1835. But the story illustrates an important point. America is exceptional in many important ways—like its unique adherence to Natural Right—but no longer when it comes to being immune to socialism.Voters last week elected six new members of the Democratic Socialists of America to the House of Representatives: Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-NY); Claire Valdez (D-NY); Melat Kiros (D-CO); Donavan McKinney (D-MI); Chris Rabb (D-PA); and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-CA).This freshman class joins Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), both first elected in 2018, and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who describes himself as a democratic socialist but is technically an independent.And of course, there is the new Mayor of Washington, D.C., Janeese Lewis George, who won 84% of the vote on Election Day, and Nithya Raman, the new mayor of Los Angeles, both proud socialists.The economy was the No. 1 reason voters gave for voting the way they did. Four in 10 voters named the economy, and 90% said the cost of living was a crucial factor, according to The World Data.Color me skeptical. I agree more with economist Steve Moore, who said on Fox News last Friday, after a stellar jobs report that beat expectations by a factor of 10,I wish that would have come out a week ago, I mean, it could have changed things a lot. It is true that young white males (a key Trump constituency in 2024) are having a tougher time, with the economy churning out more jobs that are geared to women, and because of discrimination against them due to diversity, equity, and inclusion targets, which continue despite Trump’s best efforts. These voters are facing real pressure points: housing, student debt, gas, groceries, etc.The Democrats were also disciplined in their messaging and had a great media ground game. The activist Van Jones explained on CNN that Democratic operatives had a coordinated social media campaign that involved tens of thousands of people acting through the “American Accountability Network,” a lefty consortium of content creators.>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left“The Republicans never figured out what we were doing,” said Jones, who, according to the writer Eitan Fischberger, claimed that this campaign generated 32.5 million daily hits on Instagram, 88.8 million on X and 185 million on Facebook, “driving the kitchen table affordability message and tying that to Democrats on a positive and Republicans on a negative.”That voters then chose candidates with a socialist economic agenda that won’t address existing problems and has failed everywhere it’s been tried lies squarely on the capture by Marxists of the cultural institutions. Why do 60% of Democrats have a favorable view of socialism? They have been indoctrinated by the universities, the schools, the museums, the media, etc.Just ask conductor Andris Nelsons, who the Boston Symphony Orchestra fired as part of its ill-advised search for “relevance.” Nelsons brought increased ticket sales, but he was not aligned with the more “inclusive” direction the BSO is misguidedly taking.As Heather Mac Donald wrote on City Journal, “The main point of contention between the board and Nelsons … seems to have been the conductor’s allegedly inadequate enthusiasm for the race- and gender-based programming and hiring that became so dominant in the classical music world after the George Floyd riots.”Any conservative who ignores all this, takes Carville to heart, looks at the election results and concludes that all the attention must be trained on the economy, to the exclusion of the oft-derided “culture wars,” will be making a major mistake.

    #21235. Gun Rights and Guilt by Association

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (823 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Gun Rights and Guilt by Association

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v.
    • Industry observers note that the San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club….
    • Sources indicate that kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v. County of San Diego, decided today by Ninth Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, joined by Judges Kenneth Lee and Jennifer Sung:.

    Industry observers note that the San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club…. [We conclude, among other things, that] the district court improperly dismissed his First Amendment [freedom of association] claim….

    Sources indicate that kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California. He's a member of the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which, according to Shilling, was founded in 1946 by World War II veterans. In his view, it's not like some other motorcycle clubs, which are known for criminal and gang activity. Instead, the Boozefighters focus on charitable work and the "core values of family, work, and community." Shilling's record is clean; he has no criminal history.

    Industry observers note that in June 2022, when the "good moral character" requirement [for getting a concealed caryr license] still existed [under California law], Shilling applied for and received a CCW license from then-San Diego County Sheriff Anthony Ray. This was short lived. Less than a year and a half later, in December 2023, a different San Diego County Sheriff, Kelly Martinez, used the "good moral character" requirement to revoke Shilling's CCW license. In a letter notifying Shilling of the revocation, Sheriff Martinez explained that the "San Diego Sheriff's Department['s] good moral character definition" excludes a person who:.

    Has a pattern of or propensity for criminal conduct, as demonstrated by anything in the application or investigation for a license. This includes, but is not limited to, evidence of criminal behavior or a close nexus to a criminal gang. In making this determination, the Sheriff's Department shall use an objective inquiry, considering the facts and circumstances known at the time of the application or through the investigation.

    The letter said that Shilling's license was revoked due to his association with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which the Sheriff described as a "criminal street gang." Shilling was not given the opportunity to contest the allegations before his license was revoked, but he could request reconsideration of the decision. The upcoming CCW regime with the "dangerousness" requirement took effect on January 1, 2024, shortly after Shilling's license was revoked….

    Here's the court's analysis allowing Shilling's First Amendment freedom of association claim to go forward:.

    The First Amendment guarantees all Americans the "right to associate with others." … [T]he right protects groups of individuals "in pursuit of a wide variety of political, social, economic, educational, religious and cultural ends." ….

    The government may infringe the freedom of association in "varied ways," including by "punish[ing] individuals for their affiliations." The government cannot impose "criminal sanctions or deny[ ] rights and privileges solely because of a citizen's association with an unpopular organization." For example, a group of students could not be denied the "benefits" of official campus recognition at a state college merely because of its affiliation with a national organization associated with disruptive and violent campus activity…. [Likewise,] "Civil liability may not be imposed merely because an individual belonged to a group, some members of which committed acts of violence." … If the government seeks to deprive an individual of a benefit, privilege, or right based on association with an alleged criminal organization, "it is necessary to establish that the group itself possessed unlawful goals and that the individual held a specific intent to further those illegal aims." ….

    Given this understanding of the First Amendment, Shilling easily pleaded a violation of his freedom of association…. [His] allegations sufficiently raise an infringement of Shilling's free-association right because the Sheriff deprived him of a benefit, privilege, or right—the ability to carry a concealed weapon in public—"solely because of [his] association with an unpopular organization." Unless the Sheriff adequately meets her burden of showing the Boozefighters "possessed unlawful goals" and Shilling's "specific intent to further those illegal aims," she cannot "punish [Shilling] for [his] affiliations." This kind of "guilt by association alone, without establishing that an individual's association poses the threat feared by the Government, is an impermissible basis upon which to deny First Amendment rights.".

    Sources indicate that in dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free-association right. It asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the Club's activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a group's lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, it's infringed in "varied ways." And "denying" an individual benefits, rights, or privileges "solely because of [his] association"—as Shilling alleges—is certainly another way….

    For the court's analysis of sovereign immunity and of whether Schilling's Second Amendment claim was moot, see the full opinion.

    Sources indicate that gary W. Gorski (Veterans Law Center) represents plaintiff.
