    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nikhil Gupta, also known as “Nick,” 55, an Indian national, was sentenced today to 235 months in prison for his participation in a scheme directed by a government of India employee to assassinate an attorney and political activist in the United States. In February 2026, Gupta pled guilty to a superseding indictment charging him with murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

    “Today’s prison sentence reflects the seriousness of Nikhil Gupta’s conduct and should serve as a clear warning: the Department of Justice and its law enforcement partners will pursue and hold accountable anyone who attempts to commit violence on U.S. soil or against U.S. citizens,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “While in India, Gupta helped to methodically plan the victim’s murder, believing he was beyond the reach of a U.S. court. But Gupta was wrong. Today’s sentence holds Gupta accountable for his cold and calculated plot and indicates the extent of our ability, willingness, and commitment to prosecute individuals no matter where they are located for this type of conduct.”.

    In a recent development, according to the allegations contained in the second superseding indictment, other public court documents, and statements made in court, in or about 2023, while in India, Gupta worked with others, including his co-defendant Vikash Yadav, to plot the assassination of Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, an attorney and political activist, on U.S. soil.[1] Yadav was, during all relevant times, an Indian government employee. Pannun, who is a U.S. citizen of Indian origin, is a vocal critic of the Indian government and leads a U.S.-based organization that advocates for the secession of Punjab, a state in northern India that is home to a large population of Sikhs, an ethnoreligious minority group in India. Pannun has publicly called for some or all of Punjab to secede from India and establish a Sikh sovereign state called Khalistan. The Indian government has banned Pannun and his separatist organization from India.

    Gupta is a citizen and former resident of India, who described himself in communications with Yadav and others as an international narcotics and weapons trafficker. Yadav was employed by the government of India’s Cabinet Secretariat, which houses India’s foreign intelligence service, the Research and Analysis Wing.

    In or about May 2023, Yadav recruited Gupta to orchestrate the assassination of Pannun in the United States. At Yadav’s direction, Gupta contacted an individual whom Gupta believed to be a criminal associate, but who was in fact a confidential source (CS) working with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), for assistance in contracting a hitman to murder Pannun in Fresh York City. The CS introduced Gupta to a purported hitman, who was in fact a DEA undercover officer (UC). Yadav subsequently agreed, in dealings brokered by Gupta, to pay the UC $100,000 to murder Pannun. On or about June 9, 2023, Yadav and Gupta arranged for an associate to deliver $15,000 in cash to the UC as an advance payment for the murder.

    In a recent development, in or about June 2023, in furtherance of the assassination plot, Yadav provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his home address in New York City, phone numbers associated with Pannun, and details about Pannun’s day-to-day conduct, which Gupta then passed to the UC. Gupta thereafter provided Yadav with regular updates on the assassination plot, including surveillance photographs of Pannun. Gupta directed the UC to carry out the murder as soon as possible, but Gupta also specifically instructed the UC not to commit the murder around the time of the Indian Prime Minister’s official state visit to the United States, which was scheduled to begin on or about June 20, 2023.

    Sources indicate that on or about June 18, 2023, approximately two days before the Indian Prime Minister’s state visit to the United States, masked gunmen murdered Hardeep Singh Nijjar outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia, Canada. Nijjar was an associate of Pannun, and, like Pannun, was a leader of the Sikh separatist movement and an outspoken critic of the Indian government. On or about June 19, 2023, the day after the Nijjar murder, Gupta told the UC that Nijjar “was also the target” and “we have so many targets.”  Gupta also added that, in light of Nijjar’s murder, there was “now no need to wait” on killing Pannun.

    On June 30, 2023, Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic at the request of the United States and subsequently extradited to the United States.

    The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs worked with the Czech authorities to secure the arrest and June 2024 extradition of Gupta.

    This case is being handled by the U.S. Attorney’s Office National Security and International Narcotics Unit, Violent Organizations and Crime Unit, and Narcotics Unit.

    Assistant U.S. Attorneys Camille L. Fletcher, Ashley C. Nicolas, and Alexander Li for the Southern District of Newly introduced York are in charge of the prosecution, with assistance from Trial Attorneys Kathryn DeMarco of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and A.J. Dixon of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

    #21217. Breaking: Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1391 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s a whole fresh wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases.
    • Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting.
    • Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s a whole fresh wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases. Before I get to the recommendations, you may be wondering: what time period exactly are we talking? For the purposes of this article, the medieval era is roughly defined as between 1000-1500, depending on where the characters live. For example: 15th century Italy = Renaissance. 15th century Estonia = Medieval. Burgundy, I suppose, is half and half. Periodization is a continuum much more than a series of hard stops and new beginnings, and the Renaissance is just the Middle Ages with better marketing (see Inventing the Renaissance for more on the debate).

    Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting. Most are fresh releases from this year or next year, but there are two older titles that are still recent enough to count for this trend. Books that are not yet published have their publication dates next to their publisher info. If you’ve got any Dark Ages-set mysteries to recommend to me, please comment, because I would very much like to read them.

    Sources indicate that M. T. Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.

    This came out in 2024, which I consider recent enough to include as part of this trend piece—especially when considering a medieval time scale. Also it’s awesome. In Nicked, a group of disparate travelers sets off on an odyssey of the medieval world with a common 11th century mission: they’ve been hired to steal the Anatolian relics of a powerful saint and transport them to an Italian city state in hopes of sparking more commerce from pilgrims (the medieval equivalent of taking the Dodgers from Brooklyn to LA). Along the way, they form deep bonds, some blossoming into romance, and take in the sights and sounds of the entire Mediterranean world. M. T. Anderson does that rare feat of capturing the spirit of the time, granting readers a lively, Rabelaisian interpretation of an unfairly maligned era (see history book The Bright Ages for further appreciation).

    Paul Brous, The Undying Lamb (Rising Action) Setting: Italian states, 1230.

    When a book starts with a glossary featuring words from several now-dead languages, you just know that it’s going to be impeccably researched. In Paul Brous’ medieval-set thriller, an Albigensian assassin and an English knight must protect a child with an inconvenient lineage, as a vast array of forces attempt to eliminate their vulnerable charge. Perfect for those who enjoyed Conclave, but wish it had been set waaaay further back in history.

    James Bennett, Mother of Night (Evil Twin, March 2027) Setting: Holy Roman Empire, 1291.

    In this intense work of historical horror, Saladin’s victories have sent a ragged group of crusaders fleeing from the Holy Land, their only option to board a rickety vessel soon enough broken by stormy seas. Shipwrecked and far from home, the few survivors find succor and strangeness amongst a group of miserable swamp-dwellers who warn of danger ahead; the crusaders, determined to forge ahead, do not listen, with predictably dire consequences and a surprising amount of singing.

    Ferdia Lennon, Brother Nothing (Holt, June 2027) Setting: France, 1369.

    Set just a decade before the events of Doom Painting, Brother Nothing follows a newly appointed provost and his precociously intelligent daughter as they flee plague-ridden Paris for a town in the North of France. While their latest abode does appear safe from pestilence, other dangers are many, including the perennial threat of English soldiers, an epidemic of children gone missing, and a murder pinned on a prodigal son who confesses to every possible crime— save the crime of which he is accused. As the provost uncovers layer after layer of shocking crimes and terrifying cover-ups, he and his few allies begin to suspect the entire town of conspiracy, for what reads a bit like Red Harvest, medieval style.

    It has been revealed that A.K. Blakemore, Doom Painting (Scribner, April 2027) Setting: England, 1381.

    In a recent development, I have complete trust in A.K. Blakemore’s power to render historical fiction as vivid and complex as depictions of the present, and her upcoming novel of the English Peasant’s Revolt does not disappoint. In 1381, England’s most oppressed rose up against the conditions of their serfdom, driven to rebellion by the devastation of the plague and the endless war with France. For 16 days, they challenged the notion that some should rule while others serve, embodied by Wat Tyler’s epic call-to-arms: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?” As a side note, I’ve been planning to get a tattoo of that slogan in Ye Olde Englishe font for a while now, so maybe it’s time to bite the bullet. Also the book confirms what I have always known: Wat Tyler had major sex appeal.

    Indrek Hargla, The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press) Setting: 15th Century Tallinn.

    According to recent reports, indrek Hargla’s tale of a crime-solving apothecary is based in obscure, and very real, history; the mystery unraveled by the amateur sleuth takes its jumping off point from a mysterious note in Latvian historical records, for a richly detailed and vividly imagined take on a high-water mark in Latvia’s regional influence. In The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church, the murder of an aging knight leads a city luminary towards a horrifying secret with deep implications for the city’s fragile economic status and unstable power structure.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street (Pushkin Press) Setting: Estonia, 1419.

    Hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Jo Harkin, The Pretender Setting: England, Ireland, Burgundy, 15th Century.

    At the tail end of the Wars of the Roses, an ordinary farm boy is plucked from his simple village life and trained up to become a king. He’s been swapped for a commoner at birth by his dead Earl of a father and forgotten about in the midst of internecine warfare; now, he’s the last hope for the house of York to triumph over its Tudor rivals. But does he have the stuff it takes to fight through his own doubts and become king? And will he survive the endless sacrifices demanded in his ascent to the throne? This is an excellent book to help you understand the inspirations behind Game of Thrones, or the power politics of Elaine’s kingdom in Wheel of Time.

    Katherine Arden, The Unicorn Hunter (Del Rey) Setting: Brittany, Late 15th Century.

    According to recent reports, in 15th century Brittany, a noblewoman facing an unwanted union with a far-away lord puts in motion a clever strategy to hold off the wedding: her husband-to-be must join her in a unicorn hunt in the dense, dark forest near to her castle. Soon, they find themselves transported into a magical realm beset by an ancient curse that only the lady and her wooing courtiers can break. The Unicorn Hunter takes its inspiration from the real Anne of Brittany, whose marriage to the King of France was just another method of preserving what little sovereignty her province could hold onto under the steady creep of French imperial influence, and who brought two beds to her wedding as a symbol of her independence. I think I would have quite liked Anne of Brittany—Katharine Arden certainly feels a sprightly kinship with the impish aristocrat.

    Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    There’s a fresh cozy mystery TV series called The Loch Ness Mysteries

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that as longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster.
    • In a recent development, any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me.
    • It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that as longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster. Especially me. For example, several years ago, I wrote about how, in 2016, a bunch of Norwegian scientists had sent a high-tech robot down into Loch Ness to scan the, and the robot sent back sonar scans of a creature that looked exactly like the Loch Ness monster, but actually, it turned out to be a model of the Loch Ness Monster built for the 1969 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes that had accidentally sunk during filming. So that was a bummer. A HILARIOUS bummer, but a bummer nonetheless.

    In a recent development, any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me. So you can imagine my delight when I came across news of an upcoming series from the BBC and BritBox. It’s called The Loch Ness Mysteries.

    It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.

    So, in the words of the genius who wrote the BBC’s press release, “from Scotland Yard to Scotland Scotland.”.

    Also, what’s the beautiful, brilliant, difficult detective’s name? DCI Vanessa “Nessie” Keen.

    The series will star Melissa George, Jamie Sives, and Ashley Storrie, and will be six episodes long. Ed Sellek of Sister Boniface Mysteries is the creator and head writer.

    Filming begins before the end of the year, so stay tuned!

    Sources indicate that the U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Professional Responsibility—its internal ethics watchdog—on Tuesday revealed that it has referred two of its attorneys for potential bar discipline over their use of artificial intelligence in doing their jobs.

    The lawyers’ professional conduct concerns included disclosing confidential documents to a public AI platform and ‌making misleading statements to a judge when discussing how AI-generated errors appeared in a court filing, according to a story by Reuters.

    Neither lawyer is named in the report.

    The lawyers have been referred to the DOJ’s Professional Misconduct Review Unit, which can then make recommendations to state bar authorities, according to a story by Bloomberg Law.

    #21210. 8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1444 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that I took up running in 2010.
    • According to recent reports, in reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar.
    • Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that I took up running in 2010. I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry. My partner at the time had been a serious competitive runner and believed I’d be able to just knock out an eight-minute mile.

    According to recent reports, in reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar. Somewhere in the middle of all that, I’d managed to reach number six in the UK for over-forties women’s tennis. It has gradually dawned on me that sporting success isn’t the healthy, glossy, happybodymaxx endeavour that shiny people on Instagram would have us all believe.

    Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.

    Andre Agassi, Open: An Autobiography.

    I read Open when I was on the verge of my own tennis-related nervous breakdown (alas not involving crystal meth like Agassi’s), during a heatwave in Nottingham, in a hotel room full of little flies that I’d become convinced were going to bite me and cause such a severe allergic reaction that I would die. The prologue is one of the best pieces of writing I’ve ever encountered: the extraordinary violence of a five-set tennis match, ending with the wounded competitors lying side by side, holding hands.

    Then there’s Agassi’s father’s $10,000 bet (later reduced to $500) that his nine-year-old son could beat Jim Brown, the famous American Football player. The fact that the book was ghostwritten (by the wonderful J. R. Moehringer) gives it an additional layer of weirdness and gothic edge for me.

    Rafael Nadal (with John Carlin), Rafa.

    Recent findings suggest that this is basically an OCD-fest (although officially Nadal does not have this condition) about Rafa being bullied to sporting success by his Uncle Toni. There’s a chilling story about Toni refusing to let seven-year-old Rafa have a replacement bottle of water to teach him a lesson about losing the first one (you don’t need a psychotherapist to make the link with the water bottle shenanigans on court), and another about telling him he must never make himself the center of attention, even when he was the best tennis player in the world.

    Even as an adult, Nadal describes extraordinary anxieties, including the belief that if he makes a small mistake, his mother might die. The contrast between the superhuman control Nadal displays on the tennis court and the terrifying lack of control he feels everywhere else is what makes this such a disturbing and compelling memoir.

    Serena Williams (with Daniel Paisner), My Life: Queen of the Court.

    According to recent reports, there’s a brilliant scene in the incredible Teddy Perkins episode of Atlanta where Teddy, played by Donald Glover, does a roll-call of famous fathers who have abused their children towards greatness. He mentions Joe Jackson, Tiger Woods’s father and Richard Williams.

    It has been revealed that like Andre Agassi’s father, Richard Williams was seemingly determined to create a tennis champion, trying the sport with his older daughters before it finally stuck with his youngest two, Venus and Serena. He would take them to the local tennis courts in Compton with shopping trolleys full of tennis balls. Initially, Venus was the more successful and Serena was determined to beat her own sister so she did not simply become a footnote in Venus’s story.

    Leanne Shapton, Swimming Studies.

    Sources indicate that swimming Studies was actually the book that set me off on my disastrous tennis adventure. It was a single line in it, something about how Leanne Shapton, recovered from her dark sporting childhood, was still placing in “age-group” events. It was those two words, age-group, that made me think perhaps I could resurrect my childhood tennis dreams.

    Sources indicate that when I read Swimming Studies, I was myself trying to swim seriously, but ended up with breaststroker’s knee—which is odd, as Shapton suffered exactly the same thing. I felt a little like the book was haunting me, and that I was literally absorbing its ailments quasi-gothically.

    Brad Gilbert (with Steve Jamison), Winning Ugly.

    It has been revealed that this was basically my bible during the year I played competitive tennis. Actually, that’s wrong. The Inner Game of Tennis was my bible. This was my grimoire. This may be one of the most fun dark books ever written.

    Basically, Brad Gilbert tells you how you can win at tennis (and maybe even life too)—even if you are shit. You do things like turn up early and have a hit on the court with a local coach (impossible when I tried it), then shower, change and arrive late for the match and suggest starting with no warm up. Gilbert has lots of handy hints for ways to deliberately psych out your opponents with chat specifically designed to derail them.

    Adharanand Finn, The Way of the Runner.

    Industry observers note that I really loved Finn’s previous book, Running with the Kenyans, which begins with a stirring account of him unexpectedly winning a 5K fun run. After that he goes to Kenya, meets some Massive Characters who introduce themselves with their marathon PBs, and becomes himself a more excellent runner. It’s uplifting and inspiring.

    But this book about Japanese running methods is far darker. Finn begins this one battling injury and exhaustion and then encounters the weird, workaholic training methods of the Japanese, including running with exaggeratedly short strides and accelerated cadence. There was something bleakly joyless about this book compared with the first one, but I still hoovered it up.

    Christopher McDougall, Born to Run.

    Industry observers note that reading Born to Run isn’t like reading a normal book—it’s an era of your life. My heart skips and I get goosebumps just thinking about it. The ecstatic descriptions of people for whom running is both a way of life and a form of transport, and the theories about primal living, squatting and running barefoot, would go on to underpin my philosophy of sport and life for years to come (and still do).

    After reading this book I became a primal forefoot runner. My friend Vybarr Cregan-Reid, author of Footnotes: How Running Makes Us Human, went totally barefoot, despite various broken-glass incidents in British parks. I will never forget the wonderfully compelling romance of Jenn Shelton and Billy “Bonehead” Barnett, and how they would eat pizza and drink Mountain Dew in the middle of their ultras, like running was something even Lana Del Rey could do.

    Oh, how I loved this dark and crazy book that made running seem like part religion and part disco-party where everyone successfully hides their pain.

    W. Timothy Gallwey, The Inner Game of Tennis.

    Industry observers note that the Inner Game of Tennis changed my entire life and philosophy, and there’s nothing darker than that. I found myself using it as a way of understanding EVERYTHING. The concept is that you have two selves. Self 1 and Self 2. Self 2 will quietly do things if you just leave it alone, but Self 1 is constantly judging. During my disastrous tennis adventure, I could never really get rid of Self 1 and its constant voicings of my coming glory, imminent failure, place in the rankings, what I’d tell my coach, etc.

    It has been revealed that one of the tricks Gallwey recommends is reading the writing on the tennis ball as it comes towards you. I’ve encountered this kind of method in other places too, like reciting your own phone number backwards during a panic attack.

    Sources indicate that another dark sports book I still live by is Steve Peters’s The Chimp Paradox, which has some similar ideas about quieting the crazed ego-animal within. Ultimately, if you can let Self 2 take control, you can enter the mythic space of the Zone or Flow, which is, according to Daniel Kahneman’s incredible book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the most optimal place a human can reach.

    Scarlett Thomas was born in London. She is the author of highly acclaimed contemporary cult novels including The End of Mr. Y, which was longlisted for the Orange Broadband Prize for Fiction; Oligarchy; The Seed Collectors; PopCo; The Sleepwalkers; The Runner; and the Worldquake series of middle grade books. Her novels have sold over half a million copies worldwide and been translated into twenty-six languages. Scarlett is professor of creative writing and contemporary fiction at the University of Kent. Find out more at ScarThomas.com.
